source_text: Ἔχιδνα, τὸ χαλεπώτατον τῶν ἑρπετῶν, πρὸς γάμον ἀπαντᾷ τῆς θαλασσίας μυραίνης, καὶ συριγμῷ τὴν παρουσίαν σημήνασα ἐκκαλεῖται αὐτὴν ἐκ τῶν βυθῶν πρὸς γαμικὴν συμπλοκήν. Ἡ δὲ ὑπακούει, καὶ ἑνοῦται τῷ ἰοβόλῳ. Τί βούλεταί μοι ὁ λόγος; Ὅτι κἂν τραχὺς ᾖ κἂν ἄγριος τὸ ἦθος ὁ σύνοικος, ἀνάγκη φέρειν τὴν ὁμόζυγα, καὶ ἐκ μηδεμιᾶς προφάσεως καταδέχεσθαι τὴν ἕνωσιν διασπᾶν. Πλήκτης; Ἀλλ' ἀνήρ. Πάροινος; Ἀλλ' ἡνωμένος κατὰ τὴν φύσιν. Τραχὺς καὶ δυσάρεστος; Ἀλλὰ μέλος ἤδη σὸν, καὶ μελῶν τὸ τιμιώτατον. 7.6 Ἀκουέτω δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τῆς προσηκούσης αὐτῷ παραινέσεως. Ἡ ἔχιδνα τὸν ἰὸν ἐξεμεῖ, αἰδουμένη τὸν γάμον· σὺ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπηνὲς καὶ ἀπάνθρωπον οὐκ ἀποτίθεσαι αἰδοῖ τῆς ἑνώσεως; Ἢ τάχα τὸ τῆς ἐχίδνης ὑπόδειγμα καὶ ἑτέρως ἡμῖν χρησιμεύσει, ὅτι μοιχεία τίς ἐστι τῆς φύσεως ἡ τῆς ἐχίδνης καὶ τῆς μυραίνης ἐπιπλοκή. Διδαχθήτωσαν οὖν οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπιβουλεύοντες γάμοις, ποταπῷ εἰσιν ἑρπετῷ παραπλήσιοι. Εἷς μοι σκοπὸς, πανταχόθεν οἰκοδομεῖσθαι τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν. Καταστελλέσθω τὰ πάθη τῶν ἀκολάστων, καὶ ἐγγείοις καὶ θαλαττίοις ὑποδείγμασι παιδευόμενα. Ἐνταῦθά με στῆναι τοῦ λόγου ἥ τε τοῦ σώματος καταναγκάζει ἀσθένεια, καὶ τὸ τῆς ὥρας ὀψέ· ἐπεὶ πολλὰ ἔτι προσθεῖναι εἶχον τοῖς φιληκόοις θαύματος ἄξια περὶ τῶν φυομένων ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ· περὶ θαλάσσης αὐτῆς. Πῶς εἰς ἅλας τὸ ὕδωρ πήγνυται· πῶς ὁ πολυτίμητος λίθος τὸ κουράλλιον χλόη μέν ἐστιν ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ, ἐπειδὰν δὲ εἰς τὸν ἀέρα ἐξενεχθῇ, πρὸς λίθου στερρότητα μεταπήγνυται· πόθεν τῷ εὐτελεστάτῳ ζῴῳ τῷ ὀστρέῳ τὸν βαρύτιμον μαργαρίτην ἡ φύσις ἐνέθηκεν. Ἃ γὰρ ἐπιθυμοῦσι θησαυροὶ βασιλέων, ταῦτα περὶ αἰγιαλοὺς καὶ ἀκτὰς καὶ τραχείας πέτρας διέρριπται, τοῖς ἐλύτροις τῶν ὀστρέων ἐγκείμενα. Πόθεν τὸ χρυσοῦν ἔριον αἱ πίνναι τρέφουσιν, ὅπερ οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀνθοβάφων μέχρι νῦν ἐμιμήσατο Πόθεν αἱ κόχλοι τοῖς βασιλεῦσι τὰς ἁλουργίδας χαρίζονται, αἳ καὶ τὰ ἄνθη τῶν λειμώνων τῇ εὐχροίᾳ παρέδραμον. Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα. Καὶ τί οὐ γέγονε τῶν ἀναγκαίων; τί δὲ οὐχὶ τῶν πολυτελῶν ἐχαρίσθη τῷ βίῳ; Τὰ μὲν εἰς ὑπηρεσίαν ἀνθρώπων· τὰ δὲ, εἰς θεωρίαν τοῦ περὶ τὴν κτίσιν θαύματος. Ἄλλα φοβερὰ, παιδαγωγοῦντα ἡμῶν τὸ ῥᾴθυμον. Ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὰ κήτη τὰ μεγάλα. Οὐκ ἐπειδὴ καρίδος καὶ μαινίδος μείζονα, διὰ τοῦτο μεγάλα εἴρηται, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ τοῖς μεγίστοις ὄρεσι τῷ ὄγκῳ τοῦ σώματος παρισάζεται· ἅ γε καὶ νήσων πολλάκις φαντασίαν παρέχεται, ἐπειδάν ποτε ἐπὶ τὴν ἄκραν ἐπιφάνειαν τοῦ ὕδατος ἀνανήξηται. Ταῦτα μέντοι τηλικαῦτα ὄντα οὐ περὶ ἀκτὰς, οὐδὲ αἰγιαλοὺς διατρίβει, ἀλλὰ τὸ Ἀτλαντικὸν λεγόμενον πέλαγος ἐνοικεῖ. Τοιαῦτά ἐστι τὰ πρὸς φόβον καὶ ἔκπληξιν ἡμετέραν δημιουργηθέντα ζῷα. Ἐὰν δὲ ἀκούσῃς ὅτι τὰ μέγιστα τῶν πλοίων ἡπλωμένοις ἱστίοις ἐξ οὐρίας φερόμενα τὸ μικρότατον ἰχθύδιον ἡ ἐχενηῒς οὕτω ῥᾳδίως ἵστησιν, ὥστε ἀκίνητον ἐπὶ πλεῖστον φυλάσσειν τὴν ναῦν ὥσπερ καταρριζωθεῖσαν ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ πελάγει, ἆρ' οὐχὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ μικρῷ τούτῳ τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς τοῦ κτίσαντος δυνάμεως λαμβάνεις ἀπόδειξιν; Οὐ γὰρ μόνοι ξιφίαι, καὶ πρίονες, καὶ κύνες, καὶ φάλαιναι καὶ ζύγαιναι, φοβεραὶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τρυγόνος κέντρον τῆς θαλασσίας, καὶ ταύτης νεκρᾶς, καὶ λαγωὸς ὁ θαλάσσιος, οὐχ ἧττόν ἐστι φοβερὰ, ταχεῖαν καὶ ἀπαραίτητον τὴν φθορὰν ἐπιφέροντα.
thought_title: The viper and the moray as marriage lessons
orientation: Basil is drawing moral lessons from sea creatures, now using the viper and moray eel to teach spouses to endure each other and to warn adulterers.
pass_a_gloss: The viper, the most dangerous of reptiles, goes to meet the sea moray for marriage, and having signaled its presence with a hiss, it calls her out from the depths for marital union. And she obeys, and is united with the venomous one. What does the account want for me? That even if the housemate is rough, even if wild in character, it is necessary to bear the yokemate, and from no pretext to accept breaking the union. A striker? But a husband. A drunkard? But united according to nature. Rough and hard to please? But already your member, and of members the most honored. Let the husband also hear the exhortation fitting for him. The viper vomits out its venom, respecting the marriage; do you not put away the harshness and inhumanity of the soul out of respect for the union? Or perhaps the example of the viper will serve us also in another way, because the coupling of the viper and the moray is a kind of adultery of nature. Let those who plot against the marriages of others be taught, to what kind of reptile they are similar. One goal for me, from every side to build up the Church. Let the passions of the licentious be restrained, being instructed by land and sea examples. Here to stop my discourse both the weakness of the body compels, and the lateness of the hour; since I had many things still to add for those who love to hear, worthy of wonder, about the things growing in the sea; about the sea itself. How the water is fixed into salt; how the highly valued stone, the coral, is a plant in the sea, but whenever it is brought out into the air, it is fixed into the hardness of stone; whence nature placed in the cheapest animal, the oyster, the very precious pearl. For the things which the treasuries of kings desire, these are scattered around shores and coasts and rough rocks, lying in the shells of oysters. Whence the pinnae nourish the golden wool, which no one of the dyers of flowers has imitated until now. Whence the murex shells grant to kings the purple garments, which also surpassed the flowers of the meadows in beauty of color. Let the waters bring forth. And what of necessary things has not come to be? And what of costly things has not been granted to life? Some for the service of humans; others, for contemplation of the wonder concerning creation. Others are fearful, disciplining our idleness. God made the great sea creatures. Not because they are larger than a shrimp and a small fish, for this reason are they called great, but because they are made equal to the greatest mountains in bulk of body; which indeed often provide an appearance of islands, whenever they swim up to the top surface of the water. These, however, being so great, do not spend time around coasts, nor shores, but inhabit the so-called Atlantic Ocean. Such are the animals created for our fear and astonishment. But if you hear that the largest of ships, carried by unfurled sails from a fair wind, the smallest little fish, the remora, so easily stops, so as to keep the ship motionless for the longest time, just as if rooted fast in the very sea, do you not receive in this small thing also the same proof of the power of the Creator? For not only swordfish, and sawfish, and dogfish, and whales, and hammerhead sharks are fearful, but also the sting of the stingray, of the sea one, and of this dead one, and the sea hare, is no less fearful, bringing swift and unyielding destruction.

choices.why: Standard English name for the venomous snake; keeps the definite article for the generic use.
ἀπαντᾷ means 'goes to meet'; πρὸς γάμον indicates purpose, 'for marriage'.
σύνοικος means one who dwells with another, here the spouse; 'housemate' is literal and plain.
ὁμόζυξ is literally 'yoked together'; 'yokemate' preserves the metaphor of shared yoke in marriage.
ἐχενηΐς is the remora, the fish believed to stop ships; standard English name.
λαγωός is literally 'hare'; 'sea hare' is the standard English name for the marine mollusk, which fits the context of a toxic sea creature.

pass_b_english: The viper, the most dangerous of reptiles, goes to meet the moray eel of the sea for marriage, and by hissing announces his presence, calling her up from the depths for the nuptial embrace. She obeys and unites herself with the venomous one. What does this account mean for me? That even if the housemate is harsh or savage in character, one must bear the yokemate and accept no pretext for tearing apart the union. Is he a striker? But he is a husband. Is he a drunkard? But he is united to you by nature. Is he harsh and hard to please? But he is already your member, and the most honored of your members.

Let the husband also hear the counsel that belongs to him. The viper vomits out its venom out of reverence for marriage; do you not put away the harshness and inhumanity of your soul out of reverence for the union? Perhaps the example of the viper will serve us in yet another way: the coupling of the viper and the moray eel is a kind of adultery against nature. Let those who plot against the marriages of others learn, then, what kind of reptile they resemble. My one aim is that the Church be built up from every side. Let the passions of the licentious be restrained, instructed by examples from land and sea.

Here the weakness of my body and the lateness of the hour compel me to stop my discourse, though I could still add many things worthy of wonder for those who love to hear—about the things that grow in the sea, and about the sea itself. How water solidifies into salt; how the precious stone, coral, is a plant in the sea, but when brought out into the air it hardens into the solidity of stone; from where nature placed the costly pearl inside the cheapest of creatures, the oyster. For the treasures that kings desire are scattered along shores and beaches and rough rocks, lying inside the shells of oysters. From where do the pinnae produce their golden wool, which no dyer of flowers has ever imitated until now? From where do the murex shells bestow their royal purple on kings, shells that have surpassed the flowers of the meadows in beauty of color?

"Let the waters bring forth" (Genesis 1:20). And what necessary thing has not come to be? What costly thing has not been granted to life? Some things are for the service of human beings; others are for the contemplation of the wonder in creation. Others are fearsome, disciplining our slackness.

"God made the great sea creatures" (Genesis 1:21). They are not called great merely because they are larger than a shrimp or a sprat, but because they rival the greatest mountains in the bulk of their bodies. They often present the appearance of islands whenever they swim up to the very surface of the water. Yet these creatures, enormous as they are, do not linger near shores or beaches, but inhabit the ocean called the Atlantic. Such are the animals created for our fear and astonishment.

But if you hear that the remora, the smallest little fish, so easily stops the largest ships sailing with spread sails and driven by a fair wind, keeping the vessel motionless for a very long time as if it were rooted in the middle of the sea—do you not receive in this small creature the same proof of the Creator's power? For not only swordfish, sawfish, dogfish, whales, and hammerhead sharks are fearsome, but also the stingray's barb, even when the stingray is dead, and the sea hare are no less fearsome, bringing swift and inescapable destruction.
